title: An act earns momentum by making the next choice harder than the last.
dek: Robert McKee's account of act design turns structure from a page-count formula into a chain of irreversible consequences. The useful discipline is to make each response to conflict demand more capacity, create a larger risk, and close off the easy return to the status quo.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: Progress is not the mere addition of events. Each move should alter what is possible next: raise the cost, expose a new force of opposition, or force a choice that cannot be undone. If the old move would still solve the problem, the story has not yet advanced.

canon.heading: Robert McKee: An act moves when the previous answer no longer works.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 9, "Act Design," from Robert McKee's Story, through PDF page 231. McKee describes an act as more than a stretch of runtime: it is a progression of complications in which each action meets stronger opposition, opens a wider gap between expectation and result, and forces a more consequential next choice.
canon.readerIntro: Read for the causal chain, not for a three-act template. Mark each point where a character's attempt produces an unanticipated reaction, where a former strategy is ruled out, and where the next action must ask more of the character. Then separate escalation from noise: an event is progressive only when it changes the available path forward.

blocks.label: 01 / An act is a movement through complications, not a container for pages
paragraphs: McKee frames the middle movement of story as progressive complications: a sequence that runs from the Inciting Incident toward the final Crisis/Climax. The point is not that a screenplay must display a prescribed number of acts. The point is that the protagonist's pursuit keeps meeting resistance that makes the original plan insufficient.

That definition transfers cleanly to any narrative with a decision at its center. If the next scene, beat, email, or product moment simply restates the first problem, the sequence is busy but static. The reader should be able to name what has changed in the situation and why the old answer is now too small.

blocks.label: 02 / A point of no return removes the easy move
paragraphs: McKee's first mechanism is the gap between expectation and result. A character acts to restore balance, the world reacts in an unforeseen way, and the gap signals that the initial effort will not work. The response must therefore draw on greater willpower, capacity, risk, or invention.

This is why he calls the progression a movement through points of no return. The reader does not need a louder incident; they need to see that a lesser action has become implausible. A story advances when the choice narrows because something meaningful has already happened.

blocks.label: 03 / Escalate the quality of action, not just its volume
paragraphs: McKee warns against retreating to actions of lesser quality or magnitude. The writer cannot preserve momentum by repeating a version of the move that already failed. Each new attempt must enter a more demanding level of conflict and push toward a final action beyond which the audience cannot imagine another.

For commercial storytelling, this is a useful test for a launch sequence or case study. Do not add more claims merely to prolong attention. Let a proof point create a new question, let that question reveal a real constraint, and make the next proof answer the higher-stakes objection. The sequence should earn its escalation.

blocks.label: 04 / Conflict is what carries attention through time
paragraphs: McKee calls conflict the soul of story because it makes time feel consequential. But he also distinguishes meaningful conflict from spectacle for its own sake. Opposition matters when it is honestly tied to a desire, a scarcity, or a force that can block the character's attempt to restore balance.

The practical question is therefore not, 'How can I make this more dramatic?' It is, 'What force would make the desired result genuinely harder, and what changed action would meet it?' That question protects a narrative from both flat harmony and arbitrary chaos.

blocks.label: 05 / Subplots should complicate the central movement, not decorate it
paragraphs: McKee closes by examining the relationship between a central plot and a subplot. Their strongest use is not mere variety. They can create contrast, deepen a controlling idea, raise a pressure that the central plot cannot express alone, or mirror the same dilemma on another plane.

Use that standard when you add a supporting thread to a narrative. If removing it leaves the central choice unchanged, it may be ornament. If it reframes the central desire, sharpens a contradiction, or makes the ultimate choice costlier, it belongs in the design.

passageAnchors: the Gap between expectation and result
A story must not retreat to actions of lesser quality or magnitude
closeReading: What changes when McKee defines an act by progressive complications rather than by a fixed number of pages or turning points?
Map one point of no return in McKee's sequence: what does the character expect, what reaction opens the gap, and which easier action is now eliminated?
Why is a larger action not automatically a more progressive action? Use McKee's distinction between increased magnitude and increased quality of action.
Where does McKee distinguish meaningful conflict from arbitrary spectacle, and what does that distinction imply for a commercial narrative?
Take a story, launch, or case study you are writing. Identify its central plot and one supporting thread. Does the supporting thread complicate the central choice, mirror it, or merely decorate it?
Write the next three moves in a live customer narrative. For each, name the prior action that can no longer solve the problem and the higher-stakes question the next move must answer.

principle.heading: Make each proof change the question, not merely add another answer.
principle.body: A persuasive narrative gains force when every meaningful answer alters the buyer's understanding of what remains unresolved. Begin with the live problem, introduce a credible constraint, and show how the next action changes the cost of staying put. Do not manufacture drama. Let real stakes and real trade-offs remove the easy option.
principle.example: A security product's story begins with a team overwhelmed by alert volume. A dashboard demo alone is a repeated first move. A stronger sequence shows the team filtering noise, then discovering that faster triage still leaves a blind spot in privileged access, then confronting the decision to change the approval path before an audit. Each proof creates a more specific question and makes the next action necessary.
principle.practice: Choose one narrative you are building: a landing page, sales deck, launch email, or case study. List its three most important moves. For each, write (1) the expectation, (2) the result that complicates it, (3) the old response now ruled out, and (4) the more demanding next action. Replace one repeated claim with a move that changes the stakes.

output.heading: Complete one progression map.
output.body: Keep the four-part map beside a live narrative. Your output is a sequence in which each move closes off an easy answer and earns the next, more consequential question.

signals.heading: Three signals about making progression visible before the audience loses the thread.

fieldNotes.title: Google's Pixel launch is being framed as an ecosystem event
fieldNotes.whatHappened: The Verge previewed Google's August 12 Made by Google event as a broad hardware launch, with the Pixel 11 lineup, Pixel Watch 5, Pixel Buds updates, and a possible Pixel Tag expected to appear together.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The useful marketing signal is not another phone spec sheet. Google is trying to make the next act of Pixel feel like an ecosystem progression: phone, watch, buds, tracker, and Gemini features reinforcing one another instead of asking each product to carry attention alone.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether Google makes the act structure clear at launch: which user problem gets harder without the connected system, and which device earns the next step rather than merely adding inventory.

fieldNotes.title: Foot Locker launches a new sneaker-culture brand platform
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Retail Dive reported that Foot Locker launched "It Always Will Be Foot Locker," an integrated brand platform built around its place in sneaker culture, anchored by a two-minute hero film and supported across broadcast, social, digital, out-of-home, and stores.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: This is a clean brand example of act design. Foot Locker is not trying to invent a new role; it is using archive, culture, channel breadth, and in-store proof to argue that its next act follows from the role it has already played since 1974.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether the platform moves beyond nostalgia and makes Foot Locker's current retail experience feel like the necessary home for the next sneaker-culture moment.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI is adding ad-tech primitives, not just ad inventory
fieldNotes.whatHappened: MarTech reported that OpenAI is adding technology meant to compete for ad dollars, including product carousels and AppsFlyer attribution capabilities.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: For marketers, the important shift is from attention surface to measurable sequence. Product recommendations inside ChatGPT become commercially serious only when the buyer can move from discovery to action and the advertiser can see what happened after the click.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether brands treat this as another performance channel or redesign the persuasion path around conversational qualification, comparison, and assisted purchase.
